prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its actions that made possible a new class of therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the strongest candidate on every axis I weigh. The chain from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, through the physiology of secretion and action in humans and the biology of proglucagon-derived peptides, to durable receptor agonists is unusually clear and independently confirmed. Large outcome trials by several sponsors show benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease, and the field is still expanding. It is a physiology-to-medicine story in the classic sense, and it also reaches into central appetite circuits. Five of six opening ballots, including mine, ranked it first and the sixth ranked it second, which suggests the support does not rest on one member's field. I would still defend it on the science if consensus were absent. Recognition now is timely and arguably overdue.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real. Four names compete for three slots, and the priority dispute over identifying the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov, Habener, Holst) is unsettled; Habener is not on the credited list at all. Whether a prize for basic physiology should also reward industrial design of long-acting acylated analogues (Knudsen) is a legitimate question, and leaving out the person whose work put the drug in patients' hands can look like an omission. There is also a risk that the prize is read as honouring a commercial product class instead of a discovery, and long-term safety and durability of weight loss are still being characterised.

responses.point: Ranked B046 (TNF blockade; Feldmann and Maini) first as a clean bench-to-bedside discovery with a two-name credit, and proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1, omitting Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree that TNF is a textbook case with a clean attribution, and I do not think it is a weaker discovery. It is mature, and the field has had decades to reward it. My disagreement is on the GLP-1 trio. Dropping Mojsov in favour of Knudsen reverses what I think a discovery prize should reward. The identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is the step that makes the incretin function interpretable, and the later engineering depended on it. Knudsen's work is outstanding drug design, but it sits downstream of the discovery, and the three-name cap is exactly where the committee should choose the physiological and chemical core over the industrial development. I would keep Mojsov in unless someone shows that her priority claim is weaker than Habener's, in which case the name list needs rethinking and I would want that settled before voting. B046 I keep as a credible alternative theme for a later year rather than part of this configuration.

responses.point: Ranked GLP-1 first but placed the unfolded protein response (Mori and Walter) second, as a conceptually clean and compactly attributed discovery.
responses.response: I share the view that Walter and Mori are a tidy pair and that the unfolded protein response is conceptually original. I ranked it sixth because the medical consequence is still indirect: therapeutic translation in diabetes, neurodegeneration or cancer has not arrived. That is a point about timing and fit with the prize, not about merit. I would not offer it as the second part of a two-achievement prize alongside GLP-1 now, because a two-part prize would also force us to cut the GLP-1 trio to fit three people in total. I would ask you whether you see a concrete clinical anchor for the pathway that would change that.

responses.point: Ranked GLP-1 first, optogenetics second and imatinib and BCR-ABL third, and proposed Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel for optogenetics.
responses.response: On optogenetics we agree on the trio and on the fairness problem. Leaving out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck is a serious cost, and I think it is the main reason the topic is not first for me despite its scientific merit. It is also a tool, with clinical use only beginning, so I treat it as an alternative and not as the core. On imatinib, I take the maturity and clarity argument seriously, but I put it lower. The BCR-ABL discovery behind it (Rowley and others) lies outside the credited names, and the prototype principle of targeted kinase inhibition has already been widely recognised. I would ask whether the story for Druker, Lydon and Sawyers can be framed without leaning on work that cannot be credited.

responses.point: Ranked GLP-1 first and CAR-T second, noting that Eshhar and others who conceived early chimeric receptors are not on the credited list.
responses.response: I agree with you on the gap in CAR-T attribution, and it is the main reason I rank it third and not higher. A prize for June, Sadelain and Rosenberg would implicitly settle credit for the first chimeric receptor concept without naming those who proposed it. My other reservation is Rosenberg: his adoptive cell transfer work is foundational, but its link to CAR-specific engineering is less direct than June's and Sadelain's. If the committee wants a second part to a configuration, I would still defend CAR-T over most other options on clinical impact. I do not think it needs to be paired with GLP-1 in a year when GLP-1 already fills the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide supports Mojsov alongside Holst and Drucker, given that Habener is not on the credited list.
Whether the committee prefers to credit the physiology and peptide discovery or to include the industrial drug development (Knudsen) in the third slot.
Whether a single-achievement prize is better than a two-part prize, since any second achievement would force a cut within the GLP-1 trio.
I rely on memory of the historical priority claims and have not verified them against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. My postdoctoral work with Paul Greengard and my research on striatal signalling and Parkinson's disease do not involve the GLP-1, CAR-T or optogenetics candidates, though neuroscience colleagues in the optogenetics field are close to my area, which I declare for transparency. I also have about twenty documented co-authored works with a fellow committee member, Thomas Perlmann, on subjects not related to any shortlisted candidate, and I note this for completeness. I am chair, so I should not push my own ranking beyond what the evidence supports.
